deck.audience: policy analysts and climate negotiators reviewing global CO2 emission trends and national responsibilities

brief.title: Global CO₂ Emissions: Trends, Regional Shifts, and Per Capita Inequalities
brief.one_liner: A data-driven overview of how global carbon dioxide emissions have evolved from the Industrial Revolution to 2024, highlighting regional shifts, per capita disparities, and the latest annual changes.
brief.goal: Equip the audience with a clear understanding of who emits the most CO₂ (total and per capita), how the geographic distribution of emissions has shifted over time, and what the 2024 annual change data reveals about current trajectories.

slides.title: Global CO₂ Emissions: Trends, Regional Shifts, and Per Capita Inequalities
slides.objective: Cover slide with deck title, subtitle summarizing scope (1750–2024), data source attribution (Global Carbon Budget 2025, NASA), and a striking visual element.

slides.title: Atmospheric CO₂ Reaches 429 ppm — 50% Above Pre-Industrial Levels
slides.objective: Present the latest Mauna Loa measurement (429 ppm, Feb 2026) and contextualize it against the pre-industrial baseline of ~280 ppm. Use a simple callout stat with a timeline annotation showing the acceleration since 1958.

slides.title: Global Fossil Fuel CO₂ Emissions Grew Six-Fold: 6 Billion to 35+ Billion Tonnes
slides.objective: Show the trajectory of total global CO₂ emissions from 1750 to 2024 using a line chart description. Highlight key inflection points: 6 Bt in 1950, 20 Bt by 1990, and 35+ Bt today. Reference figure_2.jpg.

slides.title: China Now Emits Over 12 Billion Tonnes — More Than Double the United States
slides.objective: Compare annual total CO₂ emissions of the top emitters (China, US, India, Germany, UK, Brazil, France) using the data table and reference figure_3.jpg. Emphasize China's steep rise post-2000 and the US decline from its ~6 Bt peak.

slides.title: Asia Now Accounts for ~50% of Global Emissions; US + Europe Below One-Third
slides.objective: Illustrate the dramatic shift in regional emission shares from 1900 (Europe + US > 90%) to 2024 (Asia ~50%, US + Europe < 33%). Use a stacked area or comparison visual description. Mention Africa and South America each at 3–4%.

slides.title: Per Capita Gap: 15 t in the US vs. 0.1 t in Chad — a 150× Disparity
slides.objective: Present per capita CO₂ emissions for selected countries using a horizontal bar chart description. Highlight the US (~15 t), Canada (~13 t), China (~9 t), EU-27 (~7 t), World average (~5 t), India (~2 t), UK (~4 t), Kenya (<1 t). Reference figure_1.jpg for the per capita line chart.

slides.title: 2024 Snapshot: US and Europe Cut Emissions While Russia and SE Asia Increase
slides.objective: Describe the 2024 annual percentage change map (figure_4.jpg). Highlight that the US and much of Europe show blue (negative change, -1% to -5%), while Russia, parts of Africa, and Southeast Asia show orange/red (positive change, +2% to +10%). Note specific regional patterns.

slides.title: Energy Mix Explains Why France Emits Far Less Per Capita Than Germany
slides.objective: Explain that countries with similar living standards can have very different per capita emissions depending on energy sources. Contrast France/UK (high nuclear and renewables, lower per capita CO₂) with Germany/Netherlands (higher fossil fuel share). Use a small comparison table.

slides.title: Key Takeaways: Emissions Are Still Rising, But the Map of Responsibility Is Shifting
slides.objective: Summarize 4–5 key findings as bullet points: (1) Global emissions exceed 35 Bt and have not yet peaked; (2) China alone emits >25% of global total; (3) Per capita inequalities remain extreme (150×); (4) US and Europe are declining but historical cumulative responsibility remains large; (5) Policy and energy mix choices — not just prosperity — determine per capita outcomes.
